blocks.prompt: The Dragon Everybody Made Up
blocks.text: Dragons are not real. But dragon stories are very real, and they are everywhere. In China, people tell of a long dragon with no wings. It swims in rivers and clouds. It brings rain to the fields. In England, people tell of a dragon with big wings. It sits on a pile of gold and guards it. In Mexico, people told of a serpent covered in green feathers. Every country made its own dragon. These lands were far apart. They still all made a dragon. People everywhere liked the idea of a big animal that could do things people could not.

3.title: The Dragon Everybody Made Up
3.subtitle: A reading and thinking sheet for ages 7 to 8
3.intro: Read the passage, then work through each part. You can look back at the passage any time.

blocks.prompt: Where Did Dragons Come From?
blocks.text: Nobody has ever found a dragon. No bones, no eggs, no tracks. And yet dragon stories turn up almost everywhere people live. That is a puzzle worth thinking about. One idea is that people found bones. Long ago, nobody knew about dinosaurs. So when a farmer dug up a huge skull with teeth like knives, he had to explain it somehow. A dragon was a good guess. In China, people have been digging up fossils for thousands of years. They called them dragon bones. A Chinese writer named Chang Qu once wrote about dragon bones dug up in Sichuan. We now think those bones came from dinosaurs. Another idea is simpler. People are scared of the same things. Snakes bite. Big cats hunt. Birds swoop down from the sky. Put those three together and you get a dragon: a fanged, clawed thing with wings. Maybe every country invented a dragon because every country was afraid of the same animals.

4.title: The Dragon Everybody Made Up
4.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: European dragon: wings, fire, stolen gold
Chinese dragon: no wings, brings the rain

Draco lizards really glide between trees

blocks.prompt: Two Dragons, Two Different Fears
blocks.text: Start with a fact that should be strange but is not: there is no such animal as a dragon, and there never was. No fossil, no skeleton, no shed skin. Yet if you travel from Wales to Poland to India to China to Mexico, you will find a dragon in the old stories of every one of them. The dragons are not the same, though, and the differences matter. The European dragon is a monster. It has wings, it breathes fire, it sleeps on stolen gold, and a knight is supposed to kill it. In Beowulf, an Old English poem written over a thousand years ago, the hero dies fighting one. The Chinese dragon, the long, is almost the opposite. It has no wings and does not need them. It coils through rivers and clouds, it carries the rain that the crops depend on, and for centuries it stood for the emperor himself. You do not kill it. You hope it is in a good mood. Why the split? Look at what each place feared. Western Europe had knights, castles, and a story habit of heroes killing monsters. China had farms that lived or died by the summer rains. A culture tends to build the creature it needs, either a beast to defeat or a power to ask for help. There is one last twist. Real animals wear the name. The Komodo dragon is a lizard three meters long that hunts deer in Indonesia. Flying dragons, lizards of the genus Draco, glide between trees on skin stretched over their ribs. We invented the dragon first. Then we went looking for it, and named the closest things we found.

5.title: The Dragon Everybody Made Up
5.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The dragon is the only imaginary animal in the Chinese zodiac
Richard Owen coined the word dinosaur in 1842
Chinese medicine ground fossils as long gu, dragon bones
Sichuan holds some of the richest dinosaur beds on Earth
Adrienne Mayor: the ancients were the first fossil hunters
Snake plus big cat plus bird of prey equals a dragon

blocks.prompt: The Best Idea About an Animal That Never Existed
blocks.text: Consider the oddness of it. The dragon is one of the most widespread ideas humans have ever had, and it is attached to an animal that has never existed. Wales put one on its flag. China put one in its zodiac, the only imaginary creature among eleven ordinary animals. Poland tells of a dragon under the hill at Krakow. India has the naga, a serpent of the deep water. Mexico had Quetzalcoatl, a serpent dressed in green feathers. These cultures did not share a library. Something else explains the pattern. One explanation is buried in the ground. For most of human history, nobody knew what a dinosaur was. The word was not coined until 1842. Before then, people still dug up bones, and the bones were enormous. A skull the length of a man, jaws lined with teeth like blades, a thigh bone too heavy to lift. Those finds demanded a story. In China, fossils were collected and ground into medicine under a name that translates as dragon bones. In the fourth century, a writer named Chang Qu recorded dragon bones unearthed in Sichuan, a province that has since produced some of the richest dinosaur beds on Earth. The historian Adrienne Mayor has argued that ancient people were, in effect, the first fossil hunters, and that some monsters in their legends are reasonable readings of the fossil evidence they had. It is a hypothesis, not a settled fact. It is still the best account anyone has offered for why the bones and the legends keep showing up in the same places. A second explanation lives in the mind rather than the dirt. Break a dragon into parts and you get a snake, a big cat, and a bird of prey: the three animals that hunted our ancestors most efficiently. A dragon is those three fears fused into one body. That would explain the pattern without anyone needing to find a single bone. Notice that neither explanation requires a dragon. Both require people. The dragon is not evidence of a lost animal. It is evidence of how good we are at reading a story into the parts of the world we cannot yet explain, and how long that story can outlive the confusion that produced it.

6.title: The Dragon Everybody Made Up
6.subtitle: A reading and analysis sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ladon guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides
Beowulf dies fighting a hoard-guarding dragon
The Chinese long is petitioned, not slain
Richard Owen coined dinosaur in 1842
Long gu: fossils ground as dragon bones
Chang Qu recorded dragon bones at Wucheng, Sichuan
The Komodo dragon got the name second

blocks.prompt: A Fossil of Human Thinking
blocks.text: Here is a fact that deserves more attention than it gets: the dragon does not exist, has never existed, and is nonetheless one of the most successful ideas in human history. It appears on the flag of Wales and in the zodiac of China. It sleeps under a hill at Krakow and coils through the rivers of Vietnam. The Greeks set one to guard the golden apples of the Hesperides and another to guard the Golden Fleece. The Aztecs honored a serpent clothed in quetzal feathers. Beowulf, written in Old English more than a thousand years ago, ends with its hero dying at the claws of one. No animal that never lived has ever been so widely believed in. Two questions follow. Why did so many separate cultures invent the same impossible creature, and why did they not invent the same one? Start with the second question, because the answer is more revealing. Western and Eastern dragons are not variations on a theme. They are opposites. The European dragon is a problem: winged, fire breathing, hoarding gold in a cave, waiting for a hero with a sword. The Chinese long has no wings, no hoard, and no interest in being killed. It moves through water and cloud, it delivers the rain the harvest depends on, and for most of two thousand years it was the emblem of the emperor. One dragon is slain. The other is petitioned. If both came from the same source, that source was not the dragon. It was the culture doing the imagining. Medieval Europe had knights and a story tradition in which virtue proves itself by killing monsters, so it built a monster worth killing. Agricultural China had a civilization staked on the timing of the summer rains, so it built a power worth asking. Each society drew the creature it needed. The first question is harder, and the most interesting answer is buried in the ground. The word dinosaur did not exist until Richard Owen coined it in 1842. For every century before that, people who dug up giant bones had to explain them with the vocabulary they had. The bones were undeniable. A skull longer than a man is tall, teeth the size of a hand, a limb bone no ox could carry. In China, such fossils were gathered and ground into medicine under the name long gu, dragon bones. In the fourth century, the writer Chang Qu recorded dragon bones unearthed at Wucheng in Sichuan, a province that has since yielded some of the richest dinosaur beds on the planet. The classical historian Adrienne Mayor has argued that ancient peoples were the first fossil hunters, and that several of their monsters are careful interpretations of the physical evidence in front of them. Note the shape of that claim. It does not say the ancients were fools. It says the opposite: that they were doing science with the only theory available. There is a second answer that needs no bones at all. Disassemble a dragon and you find a snake, a large cat, and a bird of prey: fangs, claws, and a shadow falling from above. Those are the three predators that shaped primate fear long before anyone had language to describe them. On that account, a dragon is not a misread fossil. It is a fear, assembled. Both answers share a structure worth noticing. Neither one requires a dragon. Both require people. And that is finally what the dragon is: not a lost animal, but a fossil of human thinking, preserved in stories instead of stone. We built it out of the bones we could not name and the fears we could not shake. Then, when we finally met something close, we handed the name over anyway. The largest lizard alive hunts deer on an Indonesian island. We call it a Komodo dragon. The invention came first. The animal is only the nearest thing we could find to it.
